name: Coffee for skin / Cold brew
lead: Coffee for skin refers to using coffee, including cold brew, to look better: drunk for its antioxidants and a perceived effect on skin aging, or applied as caffeine-containing creams, serums and coffee scrubs aimed at puffiness, dark circles and the look of cellulite [3][4].

Caffeine is increasingly used in cosmetics because it is biologically active and can penetrate the skin barrier; a 2013 review in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology describes topical formulations that typically contain about 3% caffeine [3]. Dermatology literature also discusses caffeine and coffee in sunscreens and other topicals [4].

Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for roughly 4 to 24 hours and has lower titratable acidity than hot coffee [1]. Studies of its antioxidant extraction compared with hot brew exist [5]. On T Nation, cold brew comes up as an energy-drink alternative rather than as a skin product [6].
infobox: Skin aging, puffiness, dark circles, cellulite look

paras: Caffeine-containing creams, serums and gels are marketed for eye-area puffiness, skin firming and cellulite, and coffee-extract ingredients are used for antioxidant and anti-aging claims [3][4]. Researchers have also tested caffeine-loaded gels for cellulite using delivery aids such as sonophoresis [7].
Some people drink coffee for its polyphenols as part of a skin-aging or photoprotection routine; surveys and epidemiological analyses of coffee intake and skin condition exist [7].

Cold water extracts fewer of the acidic oils found in hot-brewed coffee, linked to lower acidity and astringency [1]. Caffeine extracts more slowly in cold water [1]. A 2023 review compares variables affecting antioxidant extraction in cold and hot brew coffee [5].

Coffee is associated with lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality and lower type 2 diabetes risk, with possible increased fracture risk in women and pregnancy concerns [2]. Unfiltered coffee can raise LDL cholesterol [2].

A 2013 review describes caffeine's mechanisms of action and cosmetic use, noting it penetrates the skin barrier and is typically formulated near 3% [3]. A 2022 clinical study of a coffee pulp supplement reported that after four weeks skin brightness, elasticity, spotting and collagen content were slightly better than baseline (p < 0.05) [7]. A 2024 Mendelian randomization analysis examined coffee and other beverages in relation to facial skin aging, and a 2015 cross-sectional survey looked at coffee and polyphenol intake and skin photoprotection in Japanese women [7]. A 2026 review in Antioxidants summarises coffee-derived materials as showing multifunctional value against skin aging, inflammation and barrier dysfunction [7].
No published trials of cold brew specifically for skin were located.

card.summary: Coffee and cold brew pitched for skin; general health data exist but skin claims are untested here.

quick.overview:
Coffee and cold brew are discussed online as skin helpers.

General health research on coffee exists, but nothing reviewed addresses skin appearance.
quick.mechanism: Cold brew is steeped in cold water, yielding lower acidity; no skin mechanism is documented in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Caffeine can cause anxiety or sleep disruption at high intakes, and pregnancy limits apply.

angle.text: People drink coffee or use caffeine and coffee-based skincare hoping for brighter, firmer-looking skin and less visible puffiness or cellulite. Researchers have examined topical caffeine and coffee extracts, including a small trial of a coffee pulp serum.
